title: Beyond caste names
hook: Singh and Kaur were meant to replace caste surnames

segments.voice: Yesterday, craftsmen and builders, and Lalo the carpenter. Your line was builders. This week walked through Sindhi devotees, Sikligars, traders, Sikhs of Assam, Mazhabi Sikhs and builders. So many family names. Which one stayed with you? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-three.

A form on a screen. First name. Last name. Two boxes, and the second one is doing more work than it looks. In a lot of places, a last name quietly tells a stranger where your family comes from, what your great-grandparents did for a living, sometimes which well they were allowed to drink from. All week we've met Sikh communities known by a trade, a region, a history. Today a question sits under all of them. What happens to the second box when a Guru hands everyone the same name?
screen: `FIRST NAME. LAST NAME.` → `WHAT A SURNAME TELLS A STRANGER.` → `THE SAME NAME FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Begin at Anandpur, a story this path has told before. Tradition says that when Guru Gobind Singh called for heads, the five who stood up came from different families and trades, and after the Amrit each was given the same name. Singh, for the men. Kaur, for the women who took Amrit. The point wasn't decoration. In a world where a surname announced your caste, one shared name meant nobody could read your birth off it. That's today's line: one name for all. Second, the root under the name. Long before Anandpur, Guru Nanak had already chosen a side. In a line from the opening pages of the Granth, here in paraphrase, he says he keeps company with the lowest of the low, and has no wish to keep up with the great. Where the lowly are cared for, there the gaze of grace falls. A shared name is that line turned into a habit. Third, the honest part, because the week has been honest. Names didn't stop at Singh and Kaur. Some Sikh families still carry a caste or clan name after them, or a village name, and you've met communities this week who are still known by one. Some Sikhs drop the surname entirely and go by Singh or Kaur alone. Some add a village. Some keep the family name for a passport and leave it off everywhere else. Sikhs argue about this among themselves, and the argument itself shows the old ideal is still alive. Fourth, why it still matters on an ordinary day. A name is the first thing anyone learns about you. Two shared names make a stranger ask you something else first.
screen: `AT ANANDPUR, ONE NAME FOR FIVE.` · `NANAK STANDS WITH THE LOWEST.` · `SURNAMES CAME BACK, AND SIKHS ARGUE.` · `A STRANGER HAS TO ASK SOMETHING ELSE.` · then, large: `ONE NAME FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of what a name carries. Settle, and breathe. Say your own last name silently. What does it tell people before you've said a word? A country, a family, a religion, a class, a story? Some of that you may be proud of. Some of it you never chose. Hold it gently, without judging. Then let the name go for a few breaths, and just be the one breathing. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Beyond caste names. Singh and Kaur, given to every Sikh who takes Amrit, so that a surname would no longer tell anyone a person's caste. Today's word.
Your line: one name for all. Today, when you meet someone new, ask them something before you ask where they're from or what their family does. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs who take Amrit receive the names Singh or Kaur; some use them alone, and some families also keep a clan or village name, which Sikhs discuss openly among themselves.

The giving of Kaur at the first Amrit is compressed: tradition varies on whether women received Amrit and the name Kaur at the first Vaisakhi or later. The voice says 'Kaur, for the women who took Amrit' without dating it. Please confirm.
'The five came from different families and trades' is given as tradition says; the five's castes are not named.
Ang 15 ('neechaa andar neech jaat neechee hoo at neech... jithai neech samaaleean tithai nadar teree bakhsees') paraphrased; please confirm Ang and paraphrase.
